fetched_contents.text: Housing Background Farm workers commonly face substandard housing conditions. Many workers pay high prices to live in crowded, unsanitary conditions which often lack basic utilities. They also often live in isolated areas far away from vital services, such as health clinics, grocery stores, and public transportation. Farm workers live in many different types of housing which vary widely based on geographic location, immigration status, and other factors. The most common types of farm worker housing are: * Government housing: In order to qualify for affordable subsidized housing, farm workers must be documented. Many farm worker advocates estimate that around half of the farm worker population is undocumented. Even for documented farm workers, government housing is not always up to standard. In 2011, the American Public Health Association released a policy statement declaring that improving farm worker housing is a “public health imperative.” The action steps are quite hefty, calling for the collaboration with “community housing advocacy groups, nonprofit housing organizations, community development corporations, builders, homeowners, landlords, architects, and urban planners.” * Employer-owned housing: By law, growers are required to provide housing for non-immigrant seasonal workers on a special temporary visa called H-2A. For the majority of workers living in grower-owned housing, rent is deducted from the farm workers’ paycheck. Two studies from 2009 and 2013 show that labor camps that have any amount of H-2A workers are more likely to have better living conditions and better field sanitation than those without any H-2A workers present. H-2A workers account for only about 10% of the nation’s agricultural workforce. So if farm workers don’t get work alongside H-2A workers, they may find themselves with worse conditions because there is less incentive for the providers of housing to keep up to standard. Dairy and other farm employers will sometimes provide housing on or near the farm even when it isn’t required by law. For the majority of workers living in employer-owned housing, rent is deducted from the farm workers’ paycheck. * Privately rented housing: The majority of farm workers are renters and find housing through the private market. Nationwide, there is a shortage of affordable housing and no state has an adequate supply of affordable rental housing for low-income renters. For example, in California which has the most farm workers there are only 24 affordable and available rental homes per 100 extremely low income renter households. In Florida and Texas, this number is 25. This means many farm workers reside in substandard and crowded housing at inflated prices or are homeless. ---------------------------------------- Inflated Housing Prices In the case of grower-owned and other privately-owned housing, the owner can have a monopoly on available housing which allows them to overcharge. This is especially true in areas where housing options are very limited and workers have no alternative but to pay high rates. In Santa Maria, Santa Barbara County, California, an area with a high number of farm workers, the median rent was $2,999 in March 2024. The average annual pay of a farm worker in Santa Barbara County in 2024 was $41,031 or $82,062 per year for two working parents. This means half of a family’s income is going towards rent. This problem is not unique to California. Because housing is so expensive, many workers or families will pack into one house, trailer, or apartment in order to afford rent. In a survey of small Yakima Valley, WA towns, it found overcrowding in as much as 94% of farm worker households. A high ratio of farm workers to available utilities leads to health and sanitation complications. Far too many people share cooking and laundry facilities, sinks, bathrooms, and showers. The lack of hygiene facilities can promote pesticide exposure and the spread of disease. It is important for a worker who has been exposed to pesticides to be able to shower and wash their clothes, but with so many people living in one building, this can be difficult. In other places, landowners charge rent fees on a per-person basis instead of a total for the building. These per-person rates make life even more difficult for farm worker families, who have to pay separately for each child. Where population density and housing costs are high, such as in California, farm worker families migrating for work have resorted to living in tents, abandoned buildings, tool sheds, converted school buses, caves, and chicken coops. A Los Angeles Times article from July 14 2023 showcased a farm worker, Juan Flores, and his friends who came to Mecca, CA to work the harvest. They were not able to find housing, and so they lived in their trucks—facing prolonged heat without easy access to relief. Flores says, “Need makes you suffer.” ---------------------------------------- Isolation & Housing Regulation Farm worker housing, often referred to as labor camps, are often isolated as they are generally rural and near farms. This isolation limits access to resources and can lead to a decrease in quality of life. A 2015 study found that crowding, insufficient bathing facilities, pest infestation, and structural damage are common to dwellings in farm worker labor camps. The study also found that more than one third (37.8%) of the farm worker labor camps were hidden from public view. Similarly, a 2024 survey from Migrant Justice found that conditions are inadequate and unsafe for the vast majority of dairy workers, with 82% experiencing issues with predominantly employer-provided housing isolated from the community. fetched_contents.text: Rural Recognition: Affordable and Safe Transportation Options for Remote Communities More than four million Canadians live in low-density areas, which include rural, remote, Indigenous and northern communities. Most have few transportation options aside from driving a personal vehicle. For those who cannot drive because of cost, age or ability, the lack of options can exacerbate inequities and increase risks to their health and safety. To address these issues, the federal government should work with its provincial, territorial and Indigenous counterparts to develop a new vision of passenger travel in Canada, while leveraging and expanding federal infrastructure funding to close gaps in service. Although fewer people live in these areas, they are more likely to face higher transportation costs and generate more greenhouse-gas emissions per person because they must travel longer distances. Given the unique needs of rural communities, creative solutions are necessary. The absence of a reliable national transportation vision contributes to gaps in services, and the closure of vital bus routes is amplifying the problem. While the federal government has made progress on rural daily transportation needs through its Rural Transit Solutions Fund, the fund’s potential is limited because it does not cover operating costs or intercommunity routes. The Affordability Action Council recommends that the federal government: 1. Work with provinces, territories and Indigenous governments to develop a renewed national vision of passenger transportation supported by better data, research and analysis * Update the 2013 Vision for Transportation with greater emphasis on the needs of rural, remote and Indigenous communities and closing gaps in inter-regional bus and rail service * Invest in improved data collection, including a national survey to track household travel patterns that extend beyond work commutes 2. Leverage infrastructure funding and Via Rail to help close gaps in inter-regional bus and rail service * Invest in improving Via Rail’s service coverage, service offerings, frequency and fare affordability * Support provincial, territorial and Indigenous-led efforts to close gaps in bus and rail service 3. Expand the Rural Transit Solutions Fund to cover a greater range of costs, projects and applicants * Allow the fund to cover operating expenses such as leased vehicles and employee salaries * Use the fund to support intercommunity travel Rural Residents Face Increasing Transport Poverty The risk of transport poverty, or the lack of adequate transportation options to access essential services and employment, is increasing across Canada’s rural and remote communities. While transport poverty also exists in urban areas, people in rural and remote communities face additional barriers because of the long distances they must travel to access services, see a doctor or apply for social assistance (Fairbairn & Gustafson, 2006). People living in these areas rely more on cars to get to work and to access services and amen-ities in part because they must travel farther distances and because they have significantly smaller public transit systems. The increasing costs of car ownership may also limit their transportation options. People who live in rural communities typically have lower earnings compared to their urban counterparts, which may compound the problem. There are higher proportions of seniors and young people living in rural and remote communities — two groups that are often unable to drive or access a vehicle and are thus more restricted in their travel when no other transit options exist (see table 1). Very remote communities may have few roads, and northern communities face the added challenge that ice roads built on permafrost only function part of the year (Barrette & Charlebois, 2018). Climate change is increasingly creating uncertainty around the future of these ice roads. Compared to urban areas, large-scale public transportation options are less feasible in rural and remote communities. Less than 2 per cent of commuters in rural and remote regions use public transit to get to work (Larijani et al., 2019; Statistics Canada, 2023b). This is because communities are spread out over a large territory, and rural populations are smaller. Consequently, rural transportation systems are often smaller, with fewer riders, and lack the economies of scale of many urban systems. Figure 1 shows Canada’s census subdivisions grouped according to five degrees of remoteness, as defined by Statistics Canada (2022a). Canada’s population centres are shown in orange. All territory outside the orange areas is considered to be rural. Atlantic and northern Canada have a significantly higher share of rural and remote communities. Some of the most remote communities in Canada lack road and ferry access for much of the year (Transport Canada, 2020). In 2021, 117 census subdivisions, out of a total of 5,112 across Canada, were not connected to population centres via a main road or ferry network. These communities can be reached only by plane, seasonal ferries and water taxis, which in some cases don’t have a regular schedule or must be chartered (see box 1). fetched_contents.text: Barriers Encountered by Migrant Farm Workers When Accessing Health Care Services in Canada: A Scoping Review Abstract Objective This scoping review aims to examine and map existing literature about barriers encountered by migrant farm workers accessing health care services in Canada. Methods The search was conducted in multiple databases and grey literature. The PRISMA-ScR was used to document the inclusion and exclusion process. Two or more team members screened and reviewed all articles to ensure accuracy in capturing data. Synthesis 380 records were screened by examining abstracts and titles, and 325 were deemed irrelevant. Of the remaining records, 55 had full-text assessments; 16 were excluded because they did not meet the inclusion criteria. Thirty-nine articles were extracted. They represented a mix of qualitative and quantitative studies, reviews, and other forms of commentaries and analyses. The thematic analysis revealed barriers that affect migrant farm workers’ access to Canadian health care services: (1) language and literacy challenges, (2) concern of medical repatriation, (3) lack of transportation, (4) barriers to timely care and medical follow-up, (5) restrictive work schedules, and (6) health care coverage issues. Conclusion This review provides a synthesis of the barriers experienced by migrant farm workers when accessing Canadian health care services. Canadian health care policy experts and organizations where Canadian migrant farm workers seek care are encouraged to design and implement policies, practice changes and/or educational interventions to address these barriers. This review may also inform public health nursing programming to promote positive health outcomes in the migrant farm worker population. They are temporary foreign workers (TFWs) in the agricultural sector (Al-Bazz et al., 2022). Over time, MFWs have been referred to by various names, including seasonal agricultural workers, international agricultural workers, agri-food workers, and agricultural stream workers. For this scoping review, the term MFWs will be used. Canada's agricultural sector relies heavily on migrant workers in response to labour shortages to cultivate and harvest essential food to sustain the economy (Al-Bazz et al., 2022). In 2023, Canada authorized 70,267 TFW permits for the agricultural industries; most MFWs are from low and middle-income countries, consisting of Black, Latin Americans, and other racialized populations (Amnesty International, 2025). Workers typically enter Canada through the Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program (SAWP), which is part of the Primary Agriculture stream of the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP). Temporary Foreign Worker Programs Temporary Foreign Worker Programs were established in 1973 to enable Canadian employers to fill temporary positions when qualified Canadians are unavailable. Agricultural jobs must be performed on farms, nurseries, or greenhouses and include activities such as operating agricultural machinery and planting, caring for, and harvesting crops for market (Government of Canada, 2023). These programs are known to pose unique migration, health, and safety challenges for MFWs (Mayell et al., 2025). Work permits are tied to a single employer, who can revoke a worker's permit at any time for reasons like insufficient work, refusal to work excessive overtime, or health issues that prevent the worker from continuing (Mayell et al., 2025). Within the TFWPs, there are five streams: (1) Primary Agriculture (SAWP & Agricultural stream), (2) Low Wage, (3) High wage, (4) Caregivers, and (5) Global Talent. MFWs can enter Canada via the Primary Agriculture or Low Wage streams (Amnesty International, 2025). The salaries and visa lengths vary based on the stream, with SAWP being up to eight months, the Agricultural stream lasting up to three years, and the Low Wage stream offering a one-year visa (Amnesty International, 2025). It is difficult for low-skilled workers to obtain permanent residency as they face barriers to obtaining the neutral requirements, such as a diploma, education, and language proficiency (Amnesty International, 2025). The SAWP is the oldest and most established of the two programs, and was first piloted by the federal government in Ontario in 1966 with Jamaican workers (Cohen & Hjalmarson, 2020). It was subsequently extended to include participating countries such as Barbados, Trinidad and Tobago, and Mexico (Cohen & Hjalmarson, 2020). It did not take long for the program to expand from Ontario to other Canadian provinces (Cohen & Hjalmarson, 2020). Remote housing for Seasonal Agricultural Workers in Canada significantly worsens transportation access because the workers often live far from work sites, towns, and transit infrastructure. The evidence shows that rural and remote communities are especially reliant on personal vehicles, while public transit is limited and unreliable, especially in low-density areas [N2-F3]. In agricultural communities, transportation challenges are compounded by the need to coordinate transit for workers, and federal funding opportunities for improving access are explicitly mentioned in the technical assistance brief [N2-R2]. This suggests that transportation access is not only scarce but also unevenly distributed across rural and remote regions.

The distance and frequency of transportation options are central to the problem. Rural Recognition notes that fewer than 2% of commuters in rural and remote regions use public transit to get to work, partly because communities are spread out over a large territory and rural populations are smaller [N2-F3]. This scarcity of transit options makes it harder for workers to reach work sites, social activities, and essential services. The same source also says that people in these areas often rely more on cars to get to work and access services, while the lack of public transit options can restrict access to health care and social activities [N2-F3]. That means remote housing can create a “distance penalty” where workers must travel long distances without regular, frequent, or affordable transport.

Cost and reliability of connecting transport are also major barriers. Rural Recognition states that transport poverty is increasing in rural and remote communities, with people facing higher transportation costs and a greater risk of being unable to access essential services because they cannot afford adequate transportation [N2-F3]. The source also notes that people in rural and remote communities are more likely to face higher transportation costs because they must travel longer distances, and lower earnings can compound this problem [N2-F3]. The same report points out that seniors, young people, and people with disabilities are especially affected when no other transit options exist [N2-F3]. This implies that remote housing not only makes transport less frequent but also more expensive and less reliable for workers who cannot afford cars.

Work schedules strongly affect mobility. The scoping review on migrant farm workers accessing health care services identifies restrictive work schedules as one of the barriers to timely care and medical follow-up [N3-F4]. The same review notes that migrant farm workers often face language and literacy challenges, concern of medical repatriation, lack of transportation, and restrictive work schedules [N3-F4]. In the context of seasonal agricultural work, work schedules are often tied to farming cycles, which means workers may have irregular or limited hours, making it harder to plan trips to services or to coordinate with public transit. The evidence from the seasonal work schedules and employer control search also emphasizes that seasonal agricultural workers are subject to employer control and that work schedules can limit mobility [N6-R1][N6-R4]. This means remote housing may lock workers into a cycle where they can only move when work allows, reducing their ability to access services outside work hours.

Employer-controlled transport arrangements are an important feature of remote agricultural work. The evidence on employer influence on housing provision indicates that many agricultural temporary foreign workers rely on their employer to provide housing, especially because farms are typically located in rural and remote locations [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that employer-owned housing is common, and rent is often deducted from workers’ pay [N1-F1]. In the context of transport, this employer control extends beyond housing: seasonal agricultural workers are subject to employer-specific work permits that can restrict labour mobility even within Canada [N4-R4]. The temporary foreign worker guide also says that employers must provide reasonable efforts to give workers access to health care services if they are injured or become ill at work, but employers are not required to pay for transportation to get to those services [N4-F2]. This means that while employers may provide some health-related support, they are not necessarily responsible for arranging or subsidizing transport to and from services.

Overall, remote housing for Seasonal Agricultural Workers in Canada creates a layered transportation problem: long distances, unreliable and expensive public transit, restrictive work schedules, and employer-controlled arrangements all combine to reduce mobility and access to services. The evidence consistently points to transport poverty and limited public transit as the main drivers of reduced access, while employer control and seasonal scheduling amplify these barriers [N2-F3][N3-F4][N4-R4][N4-F2].

Remote housing for Seasonal Agricultural Workers in Canada is typically organized around work sites and often located far from towns and services. The evidence indicates that many agricultural temporary foreign workers live in employer-provided housing, especially because farms are typically located in rural and often remote locations [N1-F1]. This means housing is not randomly distributed across cities; it is concentrated near farms and agricultural work sites, with workers living in close proximity to the places where they work [N1-F1]. The same source also says that farm workers live in many different types of housing, which vary widely based on geographic location, immigration status, and other factors [N1-F1]. This geographic variation suggests that remote housing is not uniform across regions and worker groups.

The most common housing types for agricultural workers include employer-owned housing, government housing, and privately rented housing [N1-F1]. Employer-owned housing is especially relevant here: for non-immigrant seasonal workers, growers are required to provide housing, and in many cases, rent is deducted from the farm workers’ paycheck [N1-F1]. Government housing is another common type, but it is limited for undocumented workers, and even for documented workers, it is not always up to standard [N1-F1]. Privately rented housing is also common, but it is often scarce and expensive, especially in areas with limited affordable housing [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that employers may provide housing on or near the farm even when it is not required by law [N1-F1]. This means that employer influence on housing provision is substantial, and housing is often arranged by the employer rather than by the worker.

Geographic distribution is shaped by the remote nature of agricultural work. The NFWM evidence says that farm worker housing is often isolated because it is generally rural and near farms [N1-F1]. It also notes that many workers live in isolated areas far away from vital services such as health clinics, grocery stores, and public transportation [N1-F1]. Rural Recognition reinforces this pattern by describing low-density areas, including rural, remote, Indigenous, and northern communities, as places where people often rely on personal vehicles because of long distances and small public transit systems [N2-F3]. This suggests that remote housing is concentrated in areas that are geographically distant from towns and services, creating a “remote housing zone” around each work site rather than around urban centers.

Differences across regions and worker groups are clear. The NFWM evidence says that farm workers live in many different types of housing that vary widely by geographic location, immigration status, and other factors [N1-F1]. The same source describes high concentrations of farm workers in areas like California, where housing costs are extremely high, and workers may live in overcrowded conditions, in tents, abandoned buildings, converted school buses, caves, chicken coops, or even trucks [N1-F1]. This implies that remote housing is not just remote in a general sense; it is also highly variable by region and by the worker’s status. Undocumented workers face especially poor housing options, while documented workers may still encounter substandard government housing [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that employer-provided housing is more common in H-2A-style arrangements, and that such housing may be better conditioned when H-2A workers are present, but worse when they are not [N1-F1]. This shows that worker group composition and employer type can shape housing quality and location.

Employer influence on housing provision is central. The evidence states that many agricultural temporary foreign workers rely on their employer to provide housing [N1-F1]. The same source explains that employer-owned housing is common, and rent is often deducted from workers’ pay [N1-F1]. It also notes that employers may provide housing on or near the farm even when it is not required by law [N1-F1]. This employer control is reinforced by the policy context: the Temporary Foreign Worker Program and related programs are employer-specific, and workers may have closed work permits that are tied to a single employer [N4-R4]. In other words, the employer is not just a workplace provider; they are a major organizer of housing, and workers may have limited ability to move housing arrangements independently. The evidence also indicates that employer-specific work permits can restrict labour mobility, even within Canada [N4-R4]. So, employer influence is not only structural but also legal and administrative.

In short, remote housing for Seasonal Agricultural Workers in Canada is usually near work sites, often in employer-provided or employer-controlled housing, and often located far from towns and services [N1-F1]. It varies across regions and worker groups, with undocumented workers, low-income workers, and workers in high-cost areas facing especially poor options [N1-F1]. Employer influence is strong, and housing is often arranged around agricultural work rather than around urban centers [N1-F1][N4-R4].

Remote housing for Seasonal Agricultural Workers in Canada severely limits access to essential services such as healthcare, education, banking, and other daily services. The evidence shows that migrant farm workers often live in isolated areas far away from vital services such as health clinics, grocery stores, and public transportation [N1-F1]. Rural Recognition also states that people in rural and remote communities are more likely to face higher transportation costs and rely more on cars to get to work and access services, while the lack of public transit options can restrict access to health care and social activities [N2-F3]. This means that remote housing is not just physically distant; it also creates a barrier to regular service use and continuity.

Healthcare access and emergency response are especially constrained. The scoping review on migrant farm workers accessing health care services identifies lack of transportation as one of the barriers to timely care and medical follow-up [N3-F4]. It also notes that migrant farm workers face language and literacy challenges, concern of medical repatriation, lack of transportation, and restrictive work schedules [N3-F4]. The same review emphasizes that Canadian health care policy experts and organizations where migrant farm workers seek care are encouraged to design policies and interventions to address these barriers [N3-F4]. In practice, the evidence suggests that workers may be unable to reach clinics, get emergency care, or follow up on medical advice because they lack reliable transport. The temporary foreign worker guide adds that employers must make reasonable efforts to provide access to health care services if workers are injured or become ill at work, but employers are not required to pay for transportation to get to those services [N4-F2]. This means that emergency response is constrained by the same mobility barriers that affect daily access.

Education, banking, and other service availability are also limited. Rural Recognition says that rural and remote communities have smaller public transit systems and that people rely more on cars to access services and amenities [N2-F3]. It also notes that transport poverty increases the risk of being unable to access essential services, including social assistance [N2-F3]. While the evidence provided here does not give detailed examples of education or banking access, the general pattern is clear: remote housing and limited transit create difficulty in accessing a broad range of services beyond just healthcare. The NFWM evidence also says that many workers live in isolated areas far away from vital services such as health clinics, grocery stores, and public transportation [N1-F1]. This implies that banking, education, and other services are similarly hard to reach when workers are stranded in remote locations without reliable transport.

Barriers to regular service use and continuity are reinforced by both distance and employer control. The scoping review identifies restrictive work schedules as a barrier to timely care and medical follow-up [N3-F4]. The same review says that migrant farm workers often face language and literacy challenges, concern of medical repatriation, and restrictive work schedules [N3-F4]. In the context of remote housing, these barriers combine with the physical distance from services. If workers must travel long distances on unreliable or expensive transport, they may skip appointments, delay care, or avoid services altogether. The evidence also suggests that workers may be unable to afford cars and may be restricted by employer-specific work permits that can limit mobility [N4-R4][N4-F2]. This makes regular service use less likely and continuity harder to maintain.

Isolation and mobility limit access in several ways. The NFWM evidence states that farm worker housing is often isolated because it is generally rural and near farms [N1-F1]. It also notes that many workers live in isolated areas far away from vital services [N1-F1]. Rural Recognition adds that remote areas are less likely to have access to quality telecommunication networks that could help circumvent transportation issues [N2-F3]. This combination of geographic isolation, limited transport, and limited telecommunications means that workers may be cut off from services even when they want to access them. The evidence also points to transport poverty as a growing issue, with people in rural and remote communities facing higher transportation costs and greater risk of being unable to access essential services [N2-F3]. This means that isolation is not just a geographical condition; it is a structural constraint that limits mobility and service access.

Overall, remote housing reduces access to healthcare, education, banking, and other essential services because workers are often far from services, have limited and unreliable transport, face restrictive work schedules, and may be subject to employer control that restricts mobility [N1-F1][N2-F3][N3-F4][N4-F2]. Isolation and transport poverty make regular service use and continuity especially difficult, reinforcing the idea that remote housing is a major barrier to service access for Seasonal Agricultural Workers in Canada.

The evidence shows that work permits are employer-specific and can restrict labour mobility, even within Canada [N4-R4]. The temporary foreign worker guide also notes that employers must provide reasonable efforts to give workers access to health care services if they are injured or become ill at work, but employers are not required to pay for transportation to those services [N4-F2].
